At a time when funding streams are inadequate, expanding operators that duplicate facility and management costs should be re-examined.

open.q: Why are you running for a seat on the Chicago Board of Education?

To support our most vulnerable students, not do the opposite.

open.title: Student voice
open.q: Students have a lot to say about their school experience, from food served at school to the programs offered. How are you going to listen to students, and how will you make decisions based on their feedback?

I will establish a committee where students can bring forward concerns, develop solutions, and write resolutions for consideration by the Board, creating a direct pathway between student experiences and district policy. Student representatives will be included in discussions on issues like school climate, meals, programming and resources, so decisions reflect those most impacted. Once fully funded and with school discretionary funds, schools should consider a participatory budgeting process to engage students in what they want and need.

open.title: Improving the board
open.q: There has been some debate about board members understanding their responsibilities, which is primarily focused on passing the budget and school policies and evaluating the CEO. Name one area where you think the school board could make a major improvement in the next two years.
open.a: IL School Code (105 ILCS 5/34-18) charges our board with "general supervision and jurisdiction over the public school system of the city." At a time where our Black, immigrant, trans and queer students are being targeted by the federal government and underfunded by our state government, a narrow interpretation of this would not meet the moment. Green schools initiatives that create healthier communities, charter oversight that prevents disruption, and our commitment to Black Student Success are just three examples from the past year of key Board priorities and accomplishments. Our budget requires full-funding. Our CEO eval requires vision. Students deserve nothing less.

open.title: Teaching and learning
open.q: What is the single most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms, and how would you work to get district leaders to address it?
open.a: The most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness is whether educators have the time, resources and support to meet every student's needs. Teachers cannot deliver their best instruction when classes are overcrowded, students lack services, or staff are stretched too thin. As President, I will prioritize smaller class sizes, fully staffed special education services, adequate preparation time, and the resources educators need. When communities help identify local needs and co-create curriculum and programming with educators, students thrive. Attendance, engagement and learning all improve.

open.title: Budget
open.q: CPS is facing a budget deficit. How do you want district officials to balance the budget?
open.a: CPS is facing a budget surplus of $1 billion dollars that is owed to us from the governor and General Assembly. It should balance its budget by collecting the funding our students have been promised through EBF [the state school funding formula] and advocating for progressive revenue so the state has the resources to fully support public education. At the district level, we should build a Sustainable Community School District that expands services while reducing costs through partnerships and shared resources, like school-based health clinics at schools such as Drake Elementary. We can create stronger schools by investing smarter, not through cuts that harm students.

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: As School Board President I will partner with everyone from every sector to improve the educational experience of our students, strengthen our neighborhood schools and create quality public education in every neighborhood. I will not accept campaign contributions from billionaires who are undermining democracy or their PACs like Urban Center or Common Ground Collective who lobby to close our public schools and have opposed policies that would fund youth jobs, public safety and tax fairness in our city.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?
open.a: Families from Chicago want to stay here and families elsewhere want to move here. Access to quality public schools is a deciding factor in the city planning to make that possible. Examples like Austin High school have shown how partnerships with health clinics can bring services directly into schools, improve student wellness, and reduce costs by connecting families to resources in one trusted location. By expanding these partnerships, alongside fully funding schools, universal full-day Pre-K starting at age three, and stronger programs, we can create schools families choose and neighborhoods that thrive and grow.

open.title: Teaching and learning
open.q: What is the single most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms, and how would you work to get district leaders to address it?

open.title: Budget
open.q: CPS is facing a budget deficit. How do you want district officials to balance the budget?

Theses students will inherit the financial decisions we make. Short-term fixes that create larger problems in future budgets are not a strategy. I want a serious review of central office spending, contracts, costs, debt and programs. Every dollar we can move closer to students and classrooms should be. Voters deserve leaders who will tell them the truth and make decisions about the next decade, not the next news cycle. Fiscal responsibility and progressive values are not mutually exclusive.

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: By remembering that the job belongs to the public and the only loyalty I have is to what’s right and good for the people of my district. I will meet with a serious interest in improving Chicago schools. Good leadership requires hearing different perspectives. But listening to someone does not mean handing them your vote. As an attorney, I am trained to examine facts, question assumptions and reach conclusions based on the evidence in front of me. That is how I will approach this role. I will explain my decisions publicly and be willing to stand by them, even when the politically easier choice would be to avoid a difficult vote.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?

Families make choices based on academic quality, safety, available programs, transportation, special education services, school climate and whether they believe a school can meet their child’s needs. CPS needs to listen directly to families and respond to what they are telling us. If parents are leaving a neighborhood school because it lacks programs they want or concerns regarding academic quality, we should be asking how to bring programs and academic standards to the people. The best enrollment strategy is to build schools families want to choose, not just demand that they go there.

issues.title: Transform CPS into a Sustainable Community Schools district: the rigorous, equitable, restorative, inclusive model we dreamed of.
Uplift student and parent voices into all aspects of school life.

local.q: Please share one issue that’s a top concern for schools in your community or your elected school board voting district.
local.a: The most common concern I hear from students is the food. Data indicates that 60% eat school lunch. Serving nutritious food that is also delicious is an issue of respect: we need to see change in the upcoming contract. From parents I most often hear a desire for after-school programming till 6 p.m. so that their children are safe and continuing to learn and expand their horizons after the formal school day. From principals and LSCs [Local School Councils] most recently I hear concern about the impact of the budget cuts and the formulas for arriving at what each school gets.

yesNo.q: CPS changed its accountability policy last year to include more metrics and to get rid of an overall rating, such as an “A.” Do you want a policy that gives schools a rating?
yesNo.why: Ratings rooted in standardized testing results can be misleading. They de-emphasize many academic considerations, including quality of services to EL [English learner] students and students with IEPs [Individualized Education Programs]. They also de-emphasize the holistic nature of education, including factors like extracurriculars, arts, culturally relevant curriculum and student leadership.

yesNo.q: Should there be stricter limits on how AI and devices are used in CPS classrooms?
yesNo.why: Extensive research shows negative cognitive, physical and emotional effects from overuse of screens. No peer-reviewed studies exist of educational ed tech and guardrails for AI in CPS are insufficient. Other districts are passing policies to promote greater intentionality and CPS should do the same.

yesNo.q: Should the Chicago Board of Education continue to raise the property tax levy to the maximum every year?
yesNo.why: The property tax levy is the only thing CPS controls. Levying less than the maximum allowed leaves money on the table, which compounds year after year. That’s not fiscally responsible given the budget deficit. However, ideally the state should pass progressive revenue proposals sufficient to fully fund the EBF [Evidence-Based Funding] formula.

yesNo.q: Should CPS continue the strategy of providing an array of different types of schools (neighborhood, charter, selective, magnet) with different programs?
yesNo.why: We need to ensure that every school is what parents told us they wanted as we fought for the elected school board — high-quality, well-resourced schools in their neighborhood within walking distance. Too many neighborhood schools have long been under-resourced and we need to undo that history of harm.

yesNo.q: Do you support closing schools for any reason?
yesNo.why: No school closings. Very underenrolled schools can be turned around — witness Dyett [High School]. Closing 50 schools saved about $25 million a year, scarred neighborhoods and led to more violence. School closing is and has been an attack on the Black community. Chicago should invest in under-resourced communities and support its schools.

yesNo.q: In the last year, CPS has converted several financially struggling charters into district-run schools but let others close. This comes as new charters aren’t opening. Do you think CPS should do more to support existing charter schools?
yesNo.why: For decades, charters operated with little accountability and now many are struggling. CPS has created a new framework that couples greater financial accountability with timely support to avoid crises. We need a similar framework regarding services to EL [English learner] students and students with IEPs [Individualized Education Programs], where many charters are also falling short. Should more charter schools open in Chicago? We should not be opening schools, charter or otherwise. We should be supporting existing schools by reimagining them as community anchors, especially in Black communities where data shows enrollment decline is focused. Failure to invest in schools and communities is a driver for population decline.

open.q: Why are you running for a seat on the Chicago Board of Education?
open.a: I am running to be part of a team that pushes for the full state funding that is owed rather than austerity practices that harm low-income and Black and brown communities, that advocates for robust and authentic parent and student voice in all aspects of school life and does not settle for a handful of roundtables and surveys, and that seeks to enact a transformative vision of a system that is equitable not just in words but in reality, built on the model of Sustainable Community Schools as we dreamed it. Change can only happen through collective work.

open.title: Student voice
open.q: Students have a lot to say about their school experience, from food served at school to the programs offered. How are you going to listen to students, and how will you make decisions based on their feedback?
open.a: Listening to students is a priority for me. I met with student groups at my district’s schools, attended student roundtables and met with student groups facilitated by community organizations. Concerns I heard most often were about food, high school applications, bathrooms and mental health. I worked to uplift their concerns with limited success, which demonstrates the need for mandated processes that require student input and participation in implementation. We need to ensure adequate support for school-level student voice committees which are open to all, but also institute structures at a district level that are more inclusive and representative.

open.title: Improving the board
open.q: There has been some debate about board members understanding their responsibilities, which is primarily focused on passing the budget and school policies and evaluating the CEO. Name one area where you think the school board could make a major improvement in the next two years.
open.a: It is our job to set the vision and it is also our job to hold CPS accountable, through the superintendent. CPS has a powerful vision, embodied in its five-year strategic plan, the Whole School Safety policy and the Black Student Achievement Plan. But plans are words and we see gaps in implementation. To hold CPS accountable, we need common definitions for key elements of the vision and free exchange of information on how the vision is being realized in our schools. Achieving that would be a major improvement.

open.title: Teaching and learning
open.q: What is the single most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms, and how would you work to get district leaders to address it?
open.a: As an educator, I will argue there is no 100-word answer to this question. One thing I reflect on a lot is the data on how little students read now, how rarely they read complete works and their increasing inability to both persist at more complex reading and synthesize information from multiple sources. When I taught middle school literacy, my team built a culture of reading and collaborated to make it a joyful as well as a rigorous experience. Incorporating teaching to encourage a love of reading (and learning generally) in the strategic plan would be my priority.

open.title: Budget
open.q: CPS is facing a budget deficit. How do you want district officials to balance the budget?
open.a: By its own evidence-based funding formula, Springfield owes Chicago $1.6 billion. If mandated categoricals were fully funded and the state paid Chicago’s legacy teacher pensions the way it pays for other districts, the number shoots up to close to $2.3 billion. We need our legislators to feel pressure to pass progressive revenue, like the bills that were left on the table this past term and proposals that have been made previously. That requires a united front from CPS, board members, the city, union partners, the business community, parents and districts around the state to push Springfield to act.

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: CTU is funded by the rank-and-file teachers who work in our schools. That is a very different “special interest” than groups funded by billionaires often from outside Chicago who are interested in the financial and profit landscape. I am vision-aligned with CTU (teachers), just as I am with parents, students and community organizations in my district. Yes, I want the common good — nurses, social workers, counselors, librarians, smaller class size, sufficient resources to support English language learners and special needs students, etc. I am interdependent with teachers, parents, students and CBOs [community-based organizations] as we work collectively to improve our schools.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?
open.a: Data shows Asian and Latine enrollment holding steady and white enrollment growing. So the decline is due primarily to the exodus from the Black community — driven by disinvestment in schools and other key resources. We can strive to at least partially turn this around by reimagining schools as anchors for their communities. For example, reimagining Dyett [High School] as a Sustainable Community School has led it to go from about 15 students to 500. This will not change people’s lack of confidence in CPS’ commitment to their children overnight after decades of disinvestment and deprivation, but it’s a place to start.

local.a: Families are struggling to give their children a better life than they had. A high cost of living (driven partly by CPS mismanagement) makes raising children in Chicago harder. That debt burden is stealing opportunity from our kids. I am running to stop letting them steal from our children.

yesNo.q: CPS changed its accountability policy last year to include more metrics and to get rid of an overall rating, such as an “A.” Do you want a policy that gives schools a rating?
yesNo.why: My child is more than a test score and so is a school. But as a parent, I know families deserve a clear, honest picture of how their school is doing. Transparency helps schools identify strengths and weaknesses, target resources and improve. Accountability and nuance aren’t mutually exclusive. We need meaningful feedback to improve our schools.

yesNo.q: Should there be stricter limits on how AI and devices are used in CPS classrooms?
yesNo.why: CPS is overly reliant on devices and teachers can’t be replaced by apps. AI brings real risks to our kids’ privacy, safety and learning. Used well, it can spark creativity. However, the misuse CPS has allowed has harmed children’s learning and mental health. We need clear, enforceable limits on technology, especially for young children.

yesNo.q: Should the Chicago Board of Education continue to raise the property tax levy to the maximum every year?
yesNo.why: Every year the costs go up, and every year families feel it. CPS has leaned on reckless borrowing to cover wasteful spending, and taxpayers keep footing the bill. We should be pursuing new revenue from the state, city and private sector — not reaching into the pockets of families who are already stretched thin.

yesNo.q: Should CPS continue the strategy of providing an array of different types of schools (neighborhood, charter, selective, magnet) with different programs?
yesNo.why: There’s no one-size-fits-all in education and different school types create more opportunities than any single school could offer alone. But choice can’t become an excuse to let neighborhood schools decline. Every school must deliver an engaging, high-quality education.

yesNo.q: Do you support closing schools for any reason?
yesNo.why: Closing a school is a last resort, and only ever justified when it truly serves the students. It should never be used to strip children of their right to an education that’s meaningful, challenging and joyful. A school is the heart of a community, so the bar for closure must be high and the process open and honest.

yesNo.q: In the last year, CPS has converted several financially struggling charters into district-run schools but let others close. This comes as new charters aren’t opening. Do you think CPS should do more to support existing charter schools?
yesNo.why: We must protect all students, including those in charters. That doesn’t mean bailing out schools that failed; it means safeguarding the children in them. I warned the board repeatedly that many schools were underfunded and would close. Instead of acting, they failed to be proactive, then spent more cleaning up a mess we should have prevented. Should more charter schools open in Chicago? We need to spend money on what is best for the students.

open.q: Why are you running for a seat on the Chicago Board of Education?
open.a: I’m a former CPS student and a CPS parent. I’ve spent my adult life working to change the lives of children like me. For 10 years, I’ve fought the systemic problems inside CPS; I researched and submitted recommendations to end discriminatory practices, served on two LSCs [Local School Councils], sat on the CPS Parent Advisory Council and today I’m president of the Family Advisory Board for the Office for Students with Disabilities. Serving on the board is a natural next step. And as a scientist, I can’t help but dig for the root of a problem and build solutions that are affordable, effective and built to last.

open.title: Student voice
open.q: Students have a lot to say about their school experience, from food served at school to the programs offered. How are you going to listen to students, and how will you make decisions based on their feedback?
open.a: I’m an effective teacher, mentor and advocate for one simple reason: I actually listen to students. Serving on the board wouldn’t change that. I'll hold student forums, show up at campus events and stay in close contact with student LSC [Local School Council] representatives. And I’ll ask for their input before we make decisions that shape their lives, not after. No one understands a school day better than the kids living it and I will amplify their voice if elected.

open.title: Improving the board
open.q: There has been some debate about board members understanding their responsibilities, which is primarily focused on passing the budget and school policies and evaluating the CEO. Name one area where you think the school board could make a major improvement in the next two years.
open.a: The board should empower Local School Councils with far more control over how their budgets are allocated. The parents, teachers and neighbors closest to a school understand its needs better than anyone downtown ever could. Decisions about resources are too often made bureaucrats, disconnected from the classrooms they affect. Shifting real budget authority to LSCs over the next two years would make spending more responsive, more accountable and better aligned with what each community’s students actually need.

open.title: Teaching and learning
open.q: What is the single most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms, and how would you work to get district leaders to address it?
open.a: The single biggest factor limiting classroom effectiveness is poor leadership. CPS bureaucrats couldn’t even say what curriculum many schools were using. I called this out, along with the lack of standards in early literacy and math. We need clear, district-wide best practices for instruction, paired with a system for schools to learn from one another. When effective methods are shared and scaled, every classroom improves.

open.title: Budget
open.q: CPS is facing a budget deficit. How do you want district officials to balance the budget?
open.a: Our roughly [$730 million] deficit stems from years of wasteful spending and irresponsible borrowing. Balancing the budget requires four things: pursuing new revenue sources, eliminating waste in the central office, giving schools more control over their own budgets and reforming our vendor process to stop price gouging. We should protect classroom funding first and demand that cuts start downtown — not in our classrooms. Support our teachers and staff, cut wasteful bureaucracy.

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: I advocate for students, not special interest groups. That includes politicians, CTU [Chicago Teachers Union], business groups or charter advocates. My only test for any policy is simple: how does it affect students, and does it help build a school district that is engaging, safe and sustainable? If you’re for the students, then fight with me and we all win.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?
open.a: I’ve researched this extensively and shared my warnings with the board. Enrollment will keep declining largely because families are having fewer children. This is a demographic trend no single policy reverses. But we can compete for the students who are here. A genuinely thriving, high-quality school system draws families back into public schools. The answer isn’t managing decline; it’s building schools families need.

yesNo.q: CPS changed its accountability policy last year to include more metrics and to get rid of an overall rating, such as an “A.” Do you want a policy that gives schools a rating?

yesNo.q: Should the Chicago Board of Education continue to raise the property tax levy to the maximum every year?

yesNo.q: Should CPS continue the strategy of providing an array of different types of schools (neighborhood, charter, selective, magnet) with different programs?

yesNo.q: Do you support closing schools for any reason?

We must prioritize student transitions, preserve community connections, ensure access to quality options and center the voices of families, students and staff. yesNo.q: In the last year, CPS has converted several financially struggling charters into district-run schools but let others close. This comes as new charters aren’t opening. Do you think CPS should do more to support existing charter schools?

CPS should support charter sustainability through stronger oversight and transparency while maintaining fiscal responsibility. Should more charter schools open in Chicago? Before opening more charters, we must ensure existing schools are financially sustainable and serving all students equitably. Our focus should be strengthening all schools, charter and district, rather than expanding options without first addressing underlying challenges.

open.q: Why are you running for a seat on the Chicago Board of Education?
open.a: I’m running because I’m just getting started. My first two-year term has been about establishing the elected board’s independence, fighting for fiscal responsibility and centering student and family voices in all decisions. But I have only scratched the surface of the critical work that must happen. My full four-year term will allow me to see important initiatives through, from addressing our budget crisis to advancing authentic student voice to ensuring the board remains truly independent. I’ve built relationships with families and schools across CPS, and I understand what needs to come next. Our students deserve continuity and commitment from their elected leaders.

open.title: Student voice
open.q: Students have a lot to say about their school experience, from food served at school to the programs offered. How are you going to listen to students, and how will you make decisions based on their feedback?
open.a: I believe authentic student voice requires consistent, direct engagement. I will continue visiting schools regularly to meet with students, listen to their experiences and understand what’s working and what needs to change, from food quality to program offerings to safety concerns. To date I have visited well over 60 schools and spoken to students. I bring these conversations back to the board and advocate for student priorities in our decision-making. I also participate in student roundtables. Students are the experts on their own experience, and my role is to amplify their voices and ensure their feedback shapes the decisions we make.

open.title: Improving the board
open.q: There has been some debate about board members understanding their responsibilities, which is primarily focused on passing the budget and school policies and evaluating the CEO. Name one area where you think the school board could make a major improvement in the next two years.
open.a: In the past two years, I’ve remained steadfast in understanding governance and my board role, passing budgets, setting policies and evaluating the CEO. A major improvement the board could make is returning to this core focus rather than getting distracted by activism and external agendas. If the right people are elected in November, board members committed to student-centered governance, fiscal responsibility and independence from outside pressure, we can shift our energy toward strategic planning, budget stewardship and accountability. This requires electing candidates who understand that good governance serves students better than political grandstanding.

open.title: Teaching and learning
open.q: What is the single most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms, and how would you work to get district leaders to address it?
open.a: There are so many factors that impact instructional practices, and one of the most important is teacher quality. However, that quality is only as strong as the support system around it. Ongoing, high-quality coaching and professional development, reasonable class sizes and adequate prep time all directly shape whether even a talented teacher can deliver strong instruction day to day. As a former CPS teacher, I know this firsthand; no curriculum or mandate matters as much as whether teachers have the training, time and support to actually use it well. I will continue to prioritize funding decisions that strengthen teacher support.

open.title: Budget
open.q: CPS is facing a budget deficit. How do you want district officials to balance the budget?
open.a: CPS must balance its budget through a multi-pronged approach that protects classrooms. I will pursue every revenue source, including fighting for more state funding and TIF [Tax Increment Financing] dollars. We will continue to audit central office spending and procurement to eliminate waste that doesn’t serve students. When the moratorium lifts, I’ll have honest conversations about school consolidations prioritizing efficiency. I refuse to balance the budget on the backs of students and teachers. My role is collaborating with leadership to make difficult but strategic decisions that address our fiscal crisis while keeping resources in classrooms.

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: I appreciate the diverse support from labor unions, friends, community organizations and business leaders backing me in 2024 and today. This diversity actually ensures my independence; no single group can claim my vote because I don't rely on any one constituency. I’m an unpaid volunteer. I don't depend on any group for income or livelihood, which allows me to vote based on what’s best for students and families, not donor interests. My voting record demonstrates this independence; I’ve voted against positions supported by groups that endorsed me when I believed it was right for CPS. True independence means accountability to voters and students first.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?
open.a: Declining enrollment is one of our most serious challenges. I support strategic school consolidations that improve efficiency without harming students. These conversations must happen with full community transparency. I’m committed to working with thought partners like the University of Chicago Consortium [on School Research] to understand enrollment trends and identify evidence-based solutions. We must make our schools excellent by strengthening academics and creating safe environments so families choose CPS.

local.q: Please share one issue that’s a top concern for schools in your community or your elected school board voting district.

yesNo.q: Should there be stricter limits on how AI and devices are used in CPS classrooms?

yesNo.q: Should the Chicago Board of Education continue to raise the property tax levy to the maximum every year?

yesNo.q: Should CPS continue the strategy of providing an array of different types of schools (neighborhood, charter, selective, magnet) with different programs?

The decision should be based on student needs, community demand, and academic outcomes not ideology. Before expanding any new schools, CPS should ensure existing schools are serving students well and that any new proposal strengthens the overall system.

open.q: Why are you running for a seat on the Chicago Board of Education?

open.title: Student voice
open.q: Students have a lot to say about their school experience, from food served at school to the programs offered. How are you going to listen to students, and how will you make decisions based on their feedback?
open.a: Students experience our schools every day, so their voices matter. I will support student advisory councils, school visits, listening sessions and opportunities for students to provide direct feedback to the board. Student perspectives should help inform decisions about academics, school climate, extracurricular activities, safety and support services. At the same time, it is the responsibility of parents, educators, administrators and the board to provide a safe, supportive and challenging learning environment where every student has the opportunity to learn, grow and flourish.

open.title: Improving the board
open.q: There has been some debate about board members understanding their responsibilities, which is primarily focused on passing the budget and school policies and evaluating the CEO. Name one area where you think the school board could make a major improvement in the next two years.
open.a: The board can make the greatest improvement by strengthening transparency and accountability. Families, educators and taxpayers deserve clear information about budgets, student outcomes and district priorities. The board should set measurable goals, regularly review results and ensure every decision reflects responsible stewardship and keeps students at the center.

open.title: Teaching and learning
open.q: What is the single most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness in CPS classrooms, and how would you work to get district leaders to address it?
open.a: The most important factor impacting instructional effectiveness is ensuring educators have the support, resources and classroom conditions they need to teach successfully. Student success also depends on strong partnerships with families. The board should support teachers, promote safe and orderly classrooms and encourage meaningful family engagement so students receive consistent support both at school and at home.

open.title: Budget
open.q: CPS is facing a budget deficit. How do you want district officials to balance the budget?
open.a: Balancing the budget begins with responsible stewardship and accountability. CPS should carefully evaluate spending, eliminate inefficiencies and prioritize investments that directly improve student learning, support teachers and strengthen school safety. Every budget decision should answer one question: How does this help students succeed?

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: I will make every decision based on what is best for students, families and the community, regardless of who supports my campaign. I welcome input from educators, parents, labor organizations, businesses and community groups, but my responsibility is to the public. This is an unpaid position of public service, and my commitment is to serve the people of District 8b with transparency, integrity and an unwavering focus on student success.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?
open.a: Declining enrollment is driven by several factors, including birth rates, rising housing costs and families seeking alternatives they believe better meet their children's needs. While we cannot control every factor, we can control the quality of our schools. By improving academic outcomes, setting high expectations, expanding extracurricular and athletic opportunities and creating safe, supportive learning environments, we can rebuild confidence in CPS and make our neighborhood schools the first choice for families.

open.a: CPS must balance its budget by putting students first in every financial decision. We must address structural deficits, reduce the burden of more than $9 billion in long-term debt, and scrutinize vendor contracts, administrative spending and debt-service costs. Equity must guide our choices: historically underfunded neighborhood schools deserve targeted investments, not further cuts. When schools struggle, we should increase academic, social-emotional and operational supports — not disinvest. Board leaders must advocate for every student, in every neighborhood, with the same urgency they would for their own children. Fiscal discipline and educational equity can — and must — go hand in hand.

open.title: Independence
open.q: If you accept campaign contributions, how will you maintain independence from powerful special interests such as the CTU, business groups and charter school advocates?
open.a: My only objective is to provide the opportunity for New Sullivan Elementary to be just as competitive as Skinner West. My candidacy is driven by a mission to fiercely advocate for a high-quality, equitable education for every CPS student, centered on the fight for equitable funding. To maintain true independence from powerful special interests, my priority will always be to invest public resources directly into our neighborhood students, teachers and school infrastructure rather than charter or privatization interests.

open.title: Declining enrollment
open.q: CPS enrollment over the last decade has declined by about 20%, and demographic projections suggest it will continue to drop. How do you think the school district should address declining enrollment?
open.a: Parents will stay and invest in neighborhood schools when CPS gives them a reason to believe their children will thrive there. We must reinvest in South and West Side schools, prioritizing strong academics, special education, arts, sports, extracurriculars, safe environments, wraparound supports and modern facilities. Targeted capital and operational investments can restore trust and reduce family out-migration. Declining enrollment should be an opportunity to strengthen schools — not an excuse for cuts, closures or consolidation. CPS should invest in attracting families, improving educational opportunities and creating vibrant neighborhood schools. Our goal should be fewer empty seats — not fewer opportunities for children.
